speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
I should like to direct to the Minister of Labour a question based on recent press and radio reports that there are some 500,000 unemployed in Canada. Would the minister care to make a statement regarding this situation?

Labour Conditions
Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour!:
I want to thank my hon. friend for giving me notice of the question. I think I should say that a somewhat similar question was asked by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). She asked whether I could give percentages as well as figures. 1 hope my answer will be sufficient to answer both questions.
In the first place, operational figures are regularly compiled by the national employment service offices throughout the country on the number of applications for employment. There is also a second set of figures compiled each month by the dominion bureau of statistics on the numbers looking for work. This second figure is an estimate based on a sample survey of the labour force including persons both with and without jobs. The survey makes possible an estimate not only of the number of people who are reported as without jobs and seeking work, but also those who are away from work for a variety of reasons such as bad weather and temporary plant shutdowns.
I would like to say that because these two sets of statistics differ this does not mean that the two figures contradict one another or that they are not valuable for their own purposes. As I have indicated, they are produced in quite different ways. Because it is an administrative agency the national employment service figures will always include a number of people who, after registration, have found jobs on their own and have not notified the employment office.
On the other hand, not all unemployed persons register at an employment office. In addition, the national employment service figures of job applicants have some limitations for comparative purposes over a period of years because the coverage of the Unemployment Insurance Act has been extended a number of times in recent years. Also, the number of wage and salaried workers in the country have been steadily growing so that comparisons from one year to another need to be made with these facts in mind.
The labour force survey estimate of those "without jobs and seeking work" does not include, as I have said, a number of people away from work because of bad weather, those temporarily laid off with instructions to return to work within 30 days, or those who have worked at all, even for a few hours, during the survey week. Many of these people will, of course, be eligible for and be claiming unemployment insurance and so will be included in the employment service figures. A further reason for the difference in the two figures is that some persons, when enumerated by the labour force survey, will not be reported as seeking work even

though they are registered with the employment service. This can happen either because such persons do not have a very strong current attachment to the labour force, or because of difficulties in the precise classification of some individuals, such as elderly people, married women and persons with employment handicaps.
In an effort to remove as much confusion as possible between these two sets of figures, it was decided a year ago, after this whole question was considered carefully by an interdepartmental committee, to issue both of these figures at the same time with appropriate explanations of each. This release has been issued each month, jointly, by the Department of Labour and the dominion bureau of statistics, since December, 1952. Hon. members will understand that to get out these combined figures involves a great deal of work and the official figures can be released only once a month.
Now, to answer specifically the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) and the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) more specifically, I shall give the latest figures available in the case of both the labour force survey and the national employment service applications for work together with similar figures for earlier years.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
As I stated, this has been prepared in close collaboration with the Department of Trade and Commerce. In considering the current employment situation I would like to point out that 1953 as a whole will stand out as one of the most prosperous years on record. The high level of economic activity during 1952 continued throughout the spring and well into the summer months of 1953.
During the last few months some industries have experienced a decline in output but there is little evidence of any basic weakness in the economy. Over-all levels of income, consumer expenditures and private and public investment have continued at very high levels. In the summer and autumn of 1952 total employment expanded significantly and remained at a relatively high level during the following winter. In the fall of 1953, on the other hand, total employment declined somewhat more than seasonally, although at the beginning of November it still remained close to the high level of the previous year.
With continued growth in the labour force, unemployment has reached a level which is higher than that which prevailed in the fall of 1952. By the 10th of December 1953 applications on file at national employment service offices totalled 338,100, an increase of about
72.000	from the previous month and about
100.000	above that of a year earlier.
There has been a tendency in some quarters to use these statistics as a basis for comparing the current employment situation with that of the winter of 1949-1950. Apart from the fact that the causal factors behind the present situation are quite different from those that prevailed at that time, such as currency devaluation and import restrictions, I would like to make clear that the national employment service statistics in themselves are not a valid means of comparison. The coverage of unemployment insurance has, for instance, been extended since 1949 to cover forestry operations, and some other adjustments in coverage have been made in the intervening years. Secondly, the paid worker group has expanded during this period by about 11 per cent. These adjustments should be made before making comparisons between the two periods.
It should also be remembered that the level of economic activity in Canada at any particular time is conditioned to a marked degree by the wide variations in climate through the year. Winter weather always
Labour Conditions
results in the release of large numbers of workers from certain industries. Seasonal unemployment begins to appear with the completion of the grain harvest in the fall, it rises sharply in December and January, levels off in February and March, and then drops sharply in the spring when outdoor activity begins.
The size of this problem is not always appreciated. In the period 1947-1951 for example, construction employment declined, on the average, by over 80,000 persons between September and January. More than
60,000	persons were released from agriculture while about 45,000 workers were separated by the food and beverage industries.
Employment in sawmilling declined by about 16,000 while the cessation of inland shipping was in large part responsible for a drop of nearly 12,000 persons in water transportation. In the eight industries most susceptible to seasonable declines of this sort, the decline in employment amounted to close to 300,000 persons. The total number released because of climate and seasonal demand is probably much higher than this. However, many of these workers either retire from the labour force during the winter or find alternative employment in other activities, for varying periods, such as pulp-wood logging and other winter activities. This seasonal shift in employment patterns does not, therefore, result in an equal increase in unemployment. Nevertheless, it is clear that much of the increase in winter unemployment can be traced to seasonal declines in activity of the type mentioned. Seasonal unemployment is accentuated when offsetting winter activities such as logging fail to expand and when expansion in the manufacturing sector is easing off.
The current unemployment situation is not entirely due to the seasonal factors which I have mentioned although there are indications that the amount of purely seasonal unemployment is greater than in recent years. Other kinds of employment problems do exist in some industries in the economy and these are receiving close and continuing attention. These industries are not operating at capacity employment levels for various reasons. For some, import competition has become keener. This has been particularly true in the case of the clothing, textiles and electrical appliances industries. Others, such as sawmilling, farm implements and certain base metal producers have found world markets becoming increasingly competitive. Forestry operations in eastern Canada are currently proceeding at the low levels of last

Labour Conditions
winter, partly because of improved technology in forestry operations and partly because of the lumber and pulp markets. In most of these industries, there has been some accumulation of inventories at various levels of production and distribution, and employment in several industries is reflecting the consequent adjustments. The government is not ignoring the problems of these industries which are encountering difficulties in adjusting to a more competitive situation in both the domestic and foreign markets.
Nevertheless, I feel that it would be a mistake to draw a gloomy picture for the economy as a whole solely on the basis of the situation in which certain industries find themselves at the present time.
As my right hon. colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), pointed out to you a few weeks ago, 1953 was a remarkably prosperous year by any standard. Consumer expenditures were and are continuing at high levels while the level of overall investment in 1954 is expected to be at 1953 levels, a year in which the volume of construction activity surpassed all expectations. At the same time, while some inventory liquidation is taking place, the level of inventories in general is not so high as to cause undue alarm.
Aside from the difficulties experienced by some industries, there has been a tightening up in many sections of the economy and, as has been the experience of other trading nations, we have gradually moved from a seller's to a buyer's market. Such a change is bound to bring with it both increased emphasis on seasonality in operations and more concern on the part of employers with increasing efficiency. It is reassuring to note, however, that the basic economic strength of the economy continues to be unimpaired.
I would also like to point out that the extended coverage of unemployment insurance during the past few years has made it possible to treat intermittent increases in unemployment more effectively than could be done heretofore. The greater effectiveness of unemployment insurance has been particularly evident during the winter months when supplementary benefit provisions are in force. In February, 1951, for example, active claims were 83 per cent of job applications; by 1953 this proportion had risen to 92 per cent.
At the first sign of unemployment, one usually hears the suggestion that the government should begin a large scale public works program. Public works, in some circumstances, can be a useful way of alleviating unemployment, but they are by no means a

cure-all. There are other, and often more effective, ways of maintaining high employment levels, by various fiscal and monetary measures. At present, it seems to me that it would be unwise to embark upon a greatly expanded public works program. The construction industry is one of the most active parts of our economy and with the rate of investment expected to continue high, construction work in 1954 will probably again be at record volume. Also, employment in our seasonal industries will be expanding again sharply in the spring so that by the time any sizeable public works program was under way, it would be competing with private construction of all kinds for skilled labour and materials.
This leaves the problem of what is being done to assist those out of work, whether seasonally unemployed or otherwise. Actually, a great deal is already being done. The extended coverage of unemployment insurance during the last few years, plus the provision of supplementary unemployment insurance benefits during the first 3J months 'of each year, has done much to help ease the burden of unemployment. In the first three months of 1953 for example, a total of $63 million was paid out to workers in the form of unemployment insurance benefits. This year benefit payments will be even larger. This sum would not be offsetting income losses due to unemployment were it not for unemployment insurance. Many unemployed workers are also being assisted by family allowance payments and by old age pensions. In addition, the provincial and municipal governments are making social welfare payments which benefit those in need.
As I have said on many occasions in the past, unemployment is a problem which is the concern of all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal. The unemployment insurance program of the federal government is carrying the major share of the burden at the moment. There is, however, ia residual problem and the most effective way of solving it is through the joint efforts of the provincial and municipal governments and of the federal government.

speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. For my authority I refer to Bourinot, fourth edition, page 512. I base my argument-did somebody make some comment?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.

I base my argument on the point that you have just mentioned, Mr. Speaker, that what is now before us is merely a previous decision of this house that this resolution will be considered in committee of the whole at a later stage. As I understood it, Your Honour has said that that position having been taken by the house on a previous date, the matter is not now open for further consideration.
May I say at once that I recognize that, under a ruling given by Mr. Speaker Macdonald in, I think, the last session before the election, these resolutions are not debatable with Your Honour in the chair.
I am not for a moment going to suggest that the resolution is debatable. However, I am suggesting and arguing that the motion now made is susceptible of amendment and that an amendment can be put forward without debate.
I base my argument on the authority of Bourinot at the page to which I have already referred and on the similarity of this proceeding to the proceedings in connection with consideration of the bill. When a bill has been read a second time, the order then is that it be considered in committee of the whole. Your Honour then puts the motion: Is it agreed that I do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole upon the said bill? What is happening here is that Your Honour is putting the motion that Your Honour leave the chair for the house to go into committee of the 

whole on the said resolution. I therefore submit that the procedures in both cases are exactly similar. If you refer to page 512 of Bourinot, Your Honour will see the following passage:
When the order of the day for committee has been reached and called in due form

That is exactly what we have here. The order of the day for committee has been reached and called in due form.
-the Speaker will put the question,
"That I do now leave the chair".
The citation continues:
Now is the time to move any amendment to this question. Members opposed to the bill may move that the house resolve itself into committee on the bill that day three or six months: or may propose motions adverse to the principle or policy of the measure.
I submit that Your Honour has put the question, " 'That I do now leave the chair' for the house to go into committee on the resolution." It is agreed that the motion is not debatable. On the authority which I now cite, however, I submit that the motion is susceptible of amendment exactly as stated in Bourinot. Members opposed may move that the house resolve itself into committee at a later date or may propose motions adverse to the principle or policy of the measure.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has proposed a motion that, instead of the house going into committee at this time, consideration of the resolution be postponed until the matter has been referred to a royal commission for its consideration and report back to the house. While neither this motion nor the amendment is debatable, I submit that it is clearly in order to submit such an amendment, to put it without debate, and that then Your Honour must call the question upon the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, before you make your decision may I point out that only a few days ago, when the item was called dealing with the introduction of legislation affecting the Post Office Department, a vote was asked for immediately, Your Honour permitted that vote, and a recorded vote was taken. If nothing is before the house except that we go into committee to consider what is before us, I submit that there could have been no occasion for a recorded vote at that time to decide whether we should or should not go into committee. The procedure of this house is an ever-changing form that is moulded by the decisions here from day to day. By permitting the recorded vote only a few days ago, on the motion to introduce legislation affecting the Post Office Department, Your Honour at that time accepted the

proposition that something can and does happen between the calling of the item and the consideration of the resolution by the committee. On that basis I submit that it is quite proper that a motion now be presented to defer consideration of the item until a royal commission can be appointed and can make its appropriate report.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition will recall that at a certain period in the past these money resolutions, which had not been debatable, became debatable. That was the difficulty that confronted Mr. Speaker Macdonald when he decided that these money resolutions should not be debatable. I have here his ruling which appears in the Votes and Proceedings of March 26, 1953, and in Hansard of March 26, 1953, at pages 3293 and 3294. I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members the concluding paragraph of Mr. Speaker Macdonald's ruling, in which he said:
Accordingly in future once the house has decided that the Speaker will leave the chair at the next sitting of the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider a resolution I will put the motion when the order is called, but the motion will not be debatable-
Here I would submit to hon. members that it is a good principle of procedure that whatever is not debatable is not amendable. How can you introduce an amendment if you are not allowed to debate the question? I continue:
-although members will have the right to vote thereon.
This is where I join with the view of the Leader of the Opposition when he says that the other day I allowed a vote. That is quite normal and exactly in accordance with the ruling I have just quoted. Whenever the order is called I put the motion: Is it agreed that I do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole upon this resolution? If an hon. member says "No" then I do exactly as I did at the request of of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the other day. I say: "Those who are in favour of the motion will please say yea; those who are opposed will please say nay." If five members rise I then say: "Call in the members."
I am quite prepared to do so today just as I did in response to the request of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I am not acting today in any different manner from that which I adopted the last time. If the hon. member does not want the motion to be considered now he will probably reach the same objective by asking for a vote and voting against the motion. If the vote were
Senate and House of Commons carried in the negative the motion would not disappear from the order paper but would have to be called on some other day.
I hope I have made myself clear. The procedure relating to public bills is one that is provided for by standing orders. But when the hon. member for Kamloops contends that the procedure as to resolutions is the same as that which is to be adopted with respect to public bills I beg to disagree with him, and I should like to refer him to standing order 75 which reads as follows:
Every public bill shall be read twice in the house before committal or amendment.
That is the rule as far as public bills are concerned, but there is no such rule with respect to resolutions. This resolution, as I say, is one that appeared in Votes and Proceedings. It was called on the orders of the day and the order of the house was that at the next sitting the house should go into committee of the whole to consider it. As hon. members know, the government may call its business as it sees fit. Standing order 17, subparagraph 2, reads as follows:
Whenever government business has precedence, government orders may be called in such sequence as the government may think fit.
The acting leader of the house announced that this matter would be proceeded with this afternoon. The orders of the day were being called and the deputy clerk read the order. At this stage, after I put the motion that I do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole, the only proceeding which can take place is for hon. members to ask for a vote. Then I will ask for the yeas and nays and give my opinion as to whether the nays or the yeas have it. Therefore hon. members will realize that I cannot accept the amendment.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution proposes that the Senate and the House of Commons Act be amended to increase the indemnities paid to members of parliament, the salaries of the Speakers of the two houses of parliament, of the Deputy Speaker, of the leaders in the Senate and of the Leader of the Opposition, and that the Salaries Act also be amended to increase the salaries of ministers of the crown. It is intended, if the resolution is approved by the house, to introduce separate bills to amend each of the statutes concerned.
Before giving the reasons why the government decided to recommend these increases, I should like to say a word about what I think
1452	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons is the purpose of the parliamentary indemnity. It was never intended, and it is not now intended, that members of parliament should be salaried servants of the state. Members of parliament are representatives-that is true of members of both houses of parliament -and, to be truly representative, it is desirable that they should be drawn from a wide variety of occupations and walks of life and that they should be able to retain, while they are members of parliament, their connection with the occupation or walk of life and the area from which they were chosen to be representatives in parliament.
It is obvious, however, that if members must regularly expect to be absent from their homes or their ordinary place of residence for about six months in each year, and in some years even longer, few members can expect to derive from their normal occupations at home the income they would otherwise have.
Moreover, attendance at parliament makes it necessary for most members of parliament, those who do not habitually live in Ottawa, to provide themselves with a place to live in at Ottawa for a substantial part of each year in addition to their ordinary home residence, and with anything approaching the length of the sessions in recent years many members want to have their families with them in Ottawa and must have them with them if they are to have any family life at all. This, I happen to know, is of especial concern to members with young families and to members whose ordinary place of residence is at a long distance from Ottawa.
Then, too, it has always been considered important that members should have sufficient income to enable them and their families to live decently without having to worry about going into debt or being otherwise subject to embarrassments which might affect their objective approach to matters with which parliament has to deal in the interests of the nation. The purpose of the indemnity, therefore, seems to be to compensate members to a certain extent for the loss of ordinary income, to meet the additional and necessary expense of maintaining two places to live in and to help them to preserve their complete independence and objectivity in dealing with public affairs.
While membership in parliament should not be, and should not be regarded as being, a full-time occupation, it is essential that members should be able, without a too embarrassing loss of income, to attend the sessions of parliament for as long as sessions are necessary to meet the public needs, and at any time of the year that sessions may be really required in the public interest.


However much we may be able to improve the rules, I am sure we are all agreed that the normal annual session of parliament will in future continue to be much longer than the session extending over sixty-five days with fifty sitting days which the statute apparently contemplated and which it now provides for. It was my experience, and I am sure it was the experience of the opposition and the leaders of other groups opposite, that there are an increasing number of persons apt to make suitable and even distinguished members of this house who just cannot accept being candidates, because they feel that the present indemnities are not sufficient to enable them to support their families as they feel they can or as they feel they should support them. I know as a fact that in the last parliament, and I am sure it is also true in this one, a good many members found that even after reducing their previous standards of living quite substantially they could no longer make ends meet and they had to incur debts in spite of their modest scale of living.
Now, I cannot believe that the people of a country as great and as rich as Canada has now become really want that condition to continue, which makes it difficult for any but the fairly well to do to serve in the national parliament without having to make substantial financial sacrifices. These sacrifices sometimes amount to real hardship. Certainly such a condition would not make for truly democratic representation in parliament which the people of this country want.
My colleagues and I came to the conclusion that this problem should be tackled from two angles, and that was the reason why I stated in the national broadcast I made from Vancouver on July 9 of last year that it was our policy "to seek appropriate amendments to the rules of parliament with a view to ensuring speedier and more orderly conduct of the nation's business without any abridgement of the rights of the opposition or of any minority to give expression to its views. We believe that if men and women of ability are to continue to be attracted to public life some way must be found to reduce the length of some of the debates in parliament, and to make the conditions of membership less burdensome than they have become in recent years."
There is no question that if we can shorten the sessions, without neglecting in any way the interests of those we are sent here to represent, the burden and expense in parliament will be somewhat reduced. But I do not believe anyone seriously believes that the sessions can be sufficiently reduced in length

to make the present rate of indemnity adequate to cover the purposes to which I have referred.
It is true that in 1945 provision was made by parliament for an expense allowance of $2,000 which, in the case of the members of this house except ministers and the leader of the opposition, is not subject to income tax. That allowance was, however, intended to enable members to defray the multiplicity of out of pocket costs of visiting and representing their constituencies which no member can escape if he is to perform the proper functions expected of a parliamentary representative. It is not proposed at this time to make any change in the rate of that expense allowance.
The basic indemnity for attending the sessions has not been changed for over 30 years. It was fixed at $4,000 in 1920. In that long period the indemnity of members of parliament has lost its proper relationship with almost all other forms of compensation and with prices and costs and, we must admit it, has been considerably diminished by the high levels of direct taxation which are necessary under present-day conditions. Indemnities of members of most provincial legislatures, and of the national parliaments or legislatures of most countries comparable with Canada, have been increased to a point where ours suffer very much by comparison with the ratio that existed a generation ago.
The increase now proposed will certainly not do more than restore the relative proportions that existed 30 years ago. We are recommending that the indemnity be increased from $4,000 to $8,000 and at the same time it is proposed to change the basis of payment so as to end the situation which now exists whereby it is possible for members to receive two indemnities in a single year if it happens to be necessary to have two sessions of parliament.
It is the view of the government that the new indemnity should be high enough to compensate members for attending parliament on as many occasions and for as long a time as may be necessary to look after the interests of the public. We think it is bad for the prestige of parliament to leave any room for the suggestion that additional sessions, which are sometimes necessary in the best interests of the public, are, in fact, being held to increase the remuneration of members. We know, of course, that such is not the case but it is undesirable to leave any occasion for that kind of suggestion.
After careful consideration of all the alternatives, it seemed to us that the simplest method of making this change was to provide that the indemnity should be paid in 12
Senate and House of Commons monthly instalments in each year. It was represented to us that such an arrangement would meet the personal convenience of members in arranging their own budgets. For this parliament the 12-month period will start from the first day of this session, and the monthly payments will be practically the same as they are under the present law up to the end of the session. Then, instead of the unpaid balance being paid out immediately, it will be spread over the remaining months of the 12-month period. No further indemnity will start to accrue until November 12, 1954.
I want to emphasize, however, that the change in the basis of payment is not meant to change the character of the indemnity. It is still intended to be compensation to members for attending the sittings of parliament, and not a salary for being members of parliament. The provisions for the appropriate deductions for absences for other than accepted reasons will remain in effect.
I turn now to the second proposal in the resolution which is that the salaries of ministers of the crown and of the Speakers and leaders in the houses of parliament should be increased. These salaries have not been altered since 1920. This fact, in itself, is perhaps all the argument needed to explain why an increase in salaries might be justified at this time. I do not think anyone would question the statement that ministers of the crown have full-time jobs of an exacting character, with heavy responsibilities. Under our constitutional system, the same is true of the position of the leader of the official opposition.
I doubt if anyone who occupies one of these positions expects the remuneration to be comparable with the rewards open to persons of equal ability in private life, either in business or in the professions. I am sure no one expects, either, that the contrast will be too great. The increase proposed for ministers of the crown and the Leader of the Opposition is $5,000 a year. This would be provided under the bill to amend the Salaries Act, which would contain a provision that it would not come into force until the end of the present fiscal year, April 1, 1954. Since ministers will also receive sessional indemnities and the annual expense allowance for members of parliament, this will mean that their total annual remuneration will be $25,000, all of which will be subject to income tax. They will continue also to have to provide their own cars to get about and to receive $2,000 instead of having the use of car service provided by the government before 1931. This seems to be still a most modest amount compared with the salaries and earnings of most

Senate and House of Commons Canadians with senior executive positions in business or in the higher reaches of the professions.
There is another reason, perhaps not an important one, but still one that is worthy of some consideration, for increasing the remuneration of ministers. In the nature of things a reasonable relationship must be maintained between the remuneration of ministers and the salaries of the senior public servants. For several years past the government has been finding it increasingly difficult to provide salaries for senior public servants which will enable them to resist the inducements which are offered to many of them in other fields, and which they have been under great pressure to accept.
The recommendation also proposes that the salary of the Prime Minister shall be increased by $10,000. I must admit that I was reluctant to have that included in the suggestion that I was going to have to bring to parliament. I was reluctant to have it suggested that the differential between the remuneration of the Prime Minister and that of the other ministers should be widened, should be increased; but my colleagues were insistent that any smaller increase would not preserve a proper relationship. I am not so sure about that, because I know what my colleagues have to do, and I know what I have to do, too. Of course, these matters are not apt to be dealt with again for some time. It is 33 years or more since they were dealt with last.
It was pointed out that it would be less than fair to future holders of that office to have to make for them a change which was not felt to be the right thing to do at this time. Well, I felt I had reached an age where it was my duty to look on this matter as I would look at it if I were not the Prime Minister at the present time, and to take my share of responsibility in recommending an increase that was felt to be justified.
As I said before, these increases would not become effective until the beginning of the next fiscal year, April 1, 1954. We felt it was very desirable to have no possible suggestion that there was going to be anything retroactive in this. The starting of the new system from the first day of the session will mean that the monthly payments will be just about the same as they would be under the existing law, and that the only real difference will be postponing the paying out of the balance during any monthly instalment for the rest of the twelve-month period.
Of course, under our constitutional practice it is the exclusive responsibility of ministers of the crown to recommend expenditures,


and my colleagues and I are not seeking to escape that responsibility in making these recommendations. Hon. members will appreciate, however, that these recommendations, which affect all of us in parliament personally and directly, present an unusual situation. All of us feel reluctance to do for ourselves what we would not hesitate to do for others. However, all of us have a duty to consider first what is advisable in the interest of upholding and strengthening our democratic parliamentary institutions, and I ask every hon. member on both sides of the house to put aside all personal or partisan considerations and to approach the consideration of this resolution and the consequent legislation in an objective spirit, and deal with it not because of the way in which it may affect him personally, but in the way in which he honestly believes will be in the best interests of our Canadian parliamentary institutions.
I would say to hon. members on this side of the house that if they honestly believe these increases are not in the long run to be in the best interests of our democratic institutions, they should not feel that because I am the one recommending them at this time they should submit their judgment to mine. These matters should be dealt with exclusively on the ground that the opinion expressed by each individual member will be his opinion as to what will really in the long run serve the interests of the Canadian people whom members of parliament are here to represent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with most of the observations that the Prime Minister has made there will be general agreement in this house. Without in any way reviewing what already has taken place, we indicated a desire to follow another course. Might I say to those who indicated some hilarity about the fact that the committee procedure was not opposed that the ruling of the Speaker was that the only question before the house then was whether the Speaker should leave the chair. The Speaker has left the chair, and in committee we are discussing a resolution which says it is expedient to introduce measures to do certain things.
The Prime Minister has reviewed these things which it is intended to deal with. He has devoted some considerable time to an analysis of the position in which members of parliament now find themselves because of the greatly increased cost of living and the greatly lengthened sessions of parliament. He has indicated his belief that it is unlikely there will be a substantial reduction in the length of the session, I am sure there is general agreement that the efficiency and the dignity of parliament, and the respect of the

people of Canada for the parliament which passes the laws that affect their daily lives, do call for a recognition of the fact that it will not be possible to obtain the service of members of parliament unless the indemnity or allowance-call it what you will-has some relationship to the sacrifice that is made by their separating themselves from their ordinary place of residence, and in many instances from their families.
The Prime Minister has said that whatever indemnity or allowance is approved should not be regarded as a full-time salary. He has expressed his belief-and I think there will be agreement with the belief-that it is important that members retain their contacts with their own constituents, and that the value of their service was constantly increased and refreshed by contacts they were able to maintain with their own constituents and the people whom they serve in their own constituencies.
On the definition he has given regarding the attitude we should take toward indemnities and allowances of this kind there will not be debate. I think there will probably be agreement on the part of every member that it is most desirable that members be drawn from the widest possible variety of skills and occupations. May I say also drawn not just from a variety of those who make up the population of this country but also from the two sexes. We are doing our best on this side and we hope that the number of lady members of parliament will be increased. Possibly the recognition of the expenses to which lady members are put in the establishment of living quarters here will have some bearing on the number that may be able to offer themselves as candidates in coming elections.
There certainly will be no disagreement about the fact that members should be able to have their families with them when they are here. There certainly will be no disagreement about the fact that every hon. member of this house should be able to maintain those amenities that may be open to any hon. member. Undoubtedly the quality of service and the approach to the problems that confront us will be moulded and shaped in some substantial measure by the extent to which hon. members are able to retain their constant association with those family contacts that mean so much to every one of us. I am sure that all that is agreed upon.
Then the point is raised as to what the compensation should be. It is not a salary in the sense of a full-time salary and it is not intended to be income in the ordinary
Senate and House of Commons sense. There is a point that arises and a question that cannot be easily dismissed. It is a question which has engaged the attention of those who have been called upon to consider this subject on earlier occasions. Agreeing upon the definition of the payment and agreeing upon the general approach to this problem, we are all confronted with the question: What is the appropriate amount?
At that point we are compelled to ask ourselves: How are these figures arrived at? There may be perhaps a greater tendency on the other side to agree in the omniscience of the government without any supporting evidence than there would be on this side. The conviction that an indemnity or allowance should be added, the conviction that the kind of parliament that the people of Canada want may be helped greatly by payments that will attract all who would be willing to offer themselves, does not in itself answer that question.
On other occasions it was regarded as advisable that some steps be taken to find out what would be appropriate. I notice the Prime Minister referred to the words which he used in Vancouver in July of last year in regard to the intention of the government to take steps which would facilitate the procedure in this house and in that way make it possible for members of parliament to give more effective service. I did not notice any word in the quotation he mentioned which suggested that it was the intention of the government to make this increase in the indemnities or allowances. I do not think it would be desirable that anybody be under a misapprehension that the quotation which has been placed on the record was intended to place before the people that this subject was embraced by those words.
As the Prime Minister has pointed out, we have been told that it is not intended to change the $2,000 payment which was provided in 1945. May I read the words of the then prime minister, Mr. King, when he presented for second reading the bill which dealt with this subject:
The principle of this bill is to provide an allowance of $2,000 a year to members of parliament to enable them to defray expenses incidental to their calling as members. It provides that deductions shall be made from this amount on the basis of non-attendance of members. It also provides in the case of ministers of the crown, senators, and the hon. the leader of the opposition, that the allowance shall be regarded as taxable income. That is the extent of the measure.
It will be seen that while this was not subject to income tax in the case of hon. members of the house, it was subject to taxation in the case of ministers of the crown,

Senate and House of Commons leaders of the opposition in the House of Commons and the Senate and of members of the Senate. That very fact indicated that this was not some reserved amount and that that decision that it should not be taxable was related to the way in which it was paid and the total amount being received. Therefore the question arises in the mind of every hon. member: If there is to be an increase in the indemnity such as is proposed, should this part be exempt from taxation in any case? There are a great many Canadians who do believe that the indemnities should be increased, who want to make sure that those who serve the public in parliament are not called upon to make too great a sacrifice, but who nevertheless would be inclined to think that it would be a very healthy thing if every cent we received were subject to taxation.
Whether that contention is right or not there are a great many people who have already indicated their opinion to the effect that those who are assuming responsibility for the taxation of the people should themselves be fully conscious of the impact of that taxation on whatever they are paid. That may or may not be sound argument, but at least it should be possible to explore this in the way any matters of that kind can be explored, and the reasons for and against fully examined and consideration given as to whether a larger payment, if it is to be provided, should not be fully taxable so that there is before every hon. member of this house and of parliament a full consciousness of the impact of taxation upon the money that is received.
At least we can say this, that it is quite certain the voters of Canada would not approve a complete exemption. If they do approve of some exemption, then at what point do they think that exemption should begin? These are things that certainly call for some consideration.
The Prime Minister has said that the basic allowance of $4,000 has not been changed for thirty years. On the one hand that would seem to be a very cogent argument in support of the contention that something be done in view of the greatly changed value of the dollar in that length of time, and the greatly increased length of the sessions of this parliament. It also suggests that, if this figure has stood for thirty years, a few weeks or a few months more will not be unreasonable in arriving at a correct and sound decision as to what should be done in this particular case.
The Prime Minister has said that the government thinks it would be bad for the


prestige of parliament if there were any possibility of the suggestion that two sessions be held for the purpose of giving a higher indemnity. I am sure the Prime Minister will be the first to recall that I used this argument on an earlier occasion to express objection to the calling of special sessions which produced that result. Most certainly I agree with that statement. Most certainly I agree that whatever indemnity is paid, it should be an indemnity that is paid for a continuous session that will permit the conduct of all the public business of Canada without the possibility of some additional amount being paid under any circumstances that could bring parliament under possible suspicion of seeking to improve its own position. I was going to use another expression but I will satisfy myself with "improve its own position".
It can be said, and said very properly, that no one is taken by surprise by the introduction of this measure. Steps to increase the indemnity or allowances to members have been under consideration for some time and have been openly discussed and, shall I say, somewhat vigorously promoted. This has found its way into the press and may I say that the reports I have read have correctly interpreted the discussion that I believe has taken place. There is no surprise in regard to that. But, Mr. Chairman, I do not recall the discussion of some of these other subjects that are brought forward at this time. The discussion has related to the increase in the indemnity or allowances to members and there has been a great deal of interest shown in that subject, as members on the opposite side are well aware. I have not attempted in any way to leave the impression that there is not a general belief that indemnity and allowances should be adequate, when we decide what adequate is. That is something we should determine.
Let us remember that no hon. member can satisfy himself he is dealing with this by the same standards we would apply to ordinary legislation if he is prepared to deal with the whole subject matter of this resolution simply because he believes that the indemnity to hon. members is proper or otherwise. This resolution is a rolled-up package. This is not just a single question of indemnity to members. This rolled-up package is an interesting grab-bag and there are a number of interesting features to it. When we open the package we find that it deals with the indemnity of hon. members which has been discussed so frequently and, may I say, with a very high degree of understanding between members on both sides of the house. When I say understanding I mean understanding of the

problems, because there is one point I wish to make quite clear, Mr. Chairman. There has been no consultation in regard to this measure.
The Prime Minister very properly and very frankly has stated that the government has accepted responsibility for making this decision. But there was no prior discussion as to the wisdom of this course or the procedure to be followed. Therefore, we must examine this on the basis that the government, having accepted the responsibility of presenting this resolution and proposing legislation of this kind, is placing the duty upon hon. members of considering at this time, first, whether it is expedient that the legislation be introduced, and, second, of considering at a later date how to deal with the legislation itself if this resolution is passed. The first thing that we find-

There was no suggestion on
my part of any discourtesy on the part of the Prime Minister, but since the point has been raised I wish to keep the record quite clear. The first I knew of this, and this is no suggestion of discourtesy, was when the Prime Minister said the government took full responsibility. The first I heard of it was the day after the government had made its decision and the Prime Minister asked me to meet him in his office just before this motion was to be presented to the house and he informed me what the government intended to do. There was no consultation either as to the method or content of this resolution, and I mention that so there will be no misunderstanding on the other side or
Senate and House of Commons any suggestion that we at any time, by implication or otherwise, either approved or had an opportunity to approve of the procedure that is being followed or the details that have been given to us. In fact, I again emphasize the fact that the Prime Minister did take the position he has explained. He said to me that he would not expect me to express my opinion but that he was simply informing me of the decision for which the government took full responsibility.
The second subject that we find in this rolled-up package is indemnities for members of the Senate. Are the members of the committee fully informed as to the expenses of the members of the Senate and as to the difficulty of obtaining candidates for appointment to the Senate? I confess that I have heard no suggestion of great difficulty in obtaining members of the other house, even at the figure now being paid. I only mention this point because these, after all, are things that have to be borne in mind in deciding what is appropriate.
The next subject we find in this rolled-up package is the increase to the members of the government. We have been informed that this is to be an increase of $5,000. No matter what views may be held in any other part of the house, the Prime Minister has indicated his belief in our constitutional system and has continued a long recognition of the position of the Leader of the Opposition in the Senate and the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons and to whoever may occupy those positions from time to time has applied whatever proposal is made.
This resolution still further deals with the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker and it also provides for retroactive payments. This is quite a collection of things that we find in this rolled-up package. No; we are not just dealing with this single question of the indemnity to members. Surely no hon. member of this committee is going to go blindly ahead and make a grab for the whole thing just because he believes that part of it is right. After all in dealing with a resolution which says that it is expedient that certain things be done, as members of the House of Commons we have a responsibility to know that it is expedient. We also shall have a responsibility, when the bill is before us, to know that the contents of that bill contain figures and results which are in keeping with the situation fully examined by the measures that are provided under our parliamentary system. Therefore the modest conviction of any hon. member that he is fully entitled to the compensation provided for a member of parliament is not in itself sufficient argument to carry with it all the rest of these things

I hear somebody across the way saying "we did". They reformed it in the way they go about reforming anything. They made it completely subservient to their own party. But there are some people who do not think that is the way to make the Senate efficient within our constitution. In fact, I do not think the Prime Minister does or, speaking seriously, that any hon. member on the other side really does. Nevertheless these interjections sometimes do carry even beyond this house. We have urged that there be that long-delayed reform of the Senate that would make it possible for the members of the Senate to give the kind of service that I believe they want to give. I am satisfied that they, as Canadians, want to do the best they can for Canada, whether or not it was difficult to get them there. I do believe that this is long overdue, and that increased allowances to members of the Senate and the executive associated with the Senate also
1460	HOUSE OF
Senate and House oj Commons should be related to some of these reforms that would increase the opportunity to give effective service.
There is another point, Mr. Chairman, that I wish to make. I ask hon. members to bear this point in mind. We have taken the position over and over again, or shall I say that the government has taken the position over and over again, that it is not right for this parliament to make decisions that will increase expenditures from public funds without careful, extended and adequate consideration of all the facts. I do not need to review the number of occasions, even recently, when approval in principle was accompanied by the statement that it was essential that great responsibility be shown towards the public revenue, and that before we could justify substantial expenditure of public funds all the facts should be fully available and should be examined.
If we could justify to ourselves that explanation for delay in dealing with any other problem, then we must take sufficient time to obtain that kind of information in regard to a measure of this nature when we are going to be the beneficiaries if this bill becomes law. I repeat what was implied in the amendment I proposed earlier, but which was ruled out of order. I state my request that the government defer consideration of this measure, that it should not proceed any further at this stage or any subsequent stage without assurance that before we discuss the bill we will have an inquiry by a royal commission to go into the whole subject matter of this problem. May I add that we should have an assurance by the Prime Minister, on behalf of the government, that Senate reform will be tackled and that steps will be taken to carry out a re-organization of government along lines that have been suggested in this house from time to time. I believe this is sound business practice. When we talk about sound business practice and the recognition that you must pay the executive to do an executive job and that the return must be adequate for everyone to get the right kind of people, let us make sure we have taken the steps necessary to provide a framework within which the kind of people we want can do the kind of job the people of Canada want.
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I can only make this as a proposal. I do say I believe this is a time when great caution should be shown in doing anything that might suggest we were any less cautious in dealing with our own affairs than we were in dealing with the affairs of other people who depend upon this parliament for action of one kind or


another in relation to their daily affairs. We have people hoping for action from this government along many lines. I need not discuss them now. Every hon. member knows many subjects in regard to which the people of this country are calling for action from this government. Let us be sure that no suggestion goes out from this parliament that, while we are reluctant to act in regard to the things that affect the daily lives of our people, we will act with such speed, or with little information, when our own advantage may be concerned.
There is one way that the debate can be terminated at this point for the time being, and that would be an assurance by the Prime Minister that a royal commission will be appointed to conduct the kind of inquiry that will give us the detached and objective findings on which we could subsequently act with confidence, so that the people of Canada would believe no personal interest dictated the decisions we make here.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister, in his
remarks this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, suggested that members in all quarters of the house, and belonging to the various parties in the house, should decide what should be done on the basis of what is best for this institution and for this country. I believe that is the basis upon which we have to make a decision. I believe that we cannot shift the responsibility of a decision onto the shoulders of anyone else; that is, in effect, what we would be doing if we turned the matter over to any outside body. I say that immediately after the Leader of the Opposition has spoken.
This is a matter upon which I am certain there will be differences of approach and differences of opinion, not only amongst the members of the house but in the various parts, and amongst the people, of our country. What we have to consider is this: whether or not some increase in the indemnities paid members of parliament is warranted. Personally, I have long held, and 1 have not refrained from saying so, that some increase in the indemnities of members of parliament has been warranted for some time. I have stated that in the House of Commons on previous occasions, and I have stated it in my own constituency. In speaking to some members of this house before the general election, and one or two members of the government, concerning the possibility of an increase in the indemnities, I said I thought it would be much wiser to have the increase laid before the parliament which was dissolved last June so that they would take effect when this parliament assembled. I believe the country would have understood.

I believe candidates who were seeking election or members who were seeking reelection would have known what to expect when they got here, and would have been able to make their arrangements. However, that was not done.
The Prime Minister was good enough, as the Leader of the Opposition has indicated, in a courteous and proper manner, to ask the leaders of the opposition groups to meet him-I believe separately, for I met him separately-so that he could tell us what the government was going to propose. In doing so, he made it abundantly clear he was not asking any one of the opposition leaders to make any commitments, but he was giving us that information in order that we might think over what was to be proposed in this house. Consequently, I was able to go to my colleagues in the C.C.F. party in this house and convey to them in confidence what the Prime Minister had told me. We were, therefore, able to discuss the situation.
I want to say very clearly that most of my colleagues-and I use the word "most"-consider that some increase in the indemnity to hon. members of this house is warranted. I want to make that abundantly clear. Most of us, however, think, in discussing this, that the government's proposals this afternoon are higher than are necessary. I remember that in the parliament which was dissolved in June of last year we had six sessions. During those six sessions, which occurred in four years, those of us who were re-elected in 1949 received on an average $6,000 for the four years; that is, the total indemnities that were paid to us in the four years amounted to $24,000, which gave us $6,000 a year. In addition, of course, we got the expense money which, if added to the total, would mean that on the average hon. members received in the last parliament almost $8,000 for each of the four years we were here.
I want to say to the Prime Minister and to the government that we believe that was ample; we believe that is about what should have been proposed now. There may be differences of opinion regarding that, differences of opinion among my own friends, but most of us believe that. I say that, probably because of the experience we had over the last four years, we feel that that would have been the right amount, in other words that the total indemnity proposed should have been $6,000.
The government has decided-and I understand the reason-to maintain the $2,000 expense allowance. The reason is that we passed an amendment to the Income Tax Act, and I believe all the legislatures followed suit, making one-third of the indemnity
Senate and House of Commons exempt from income tax, and many of the municipal bodies in the country have followed the examples of this parliament and the legislatures. I can quite understand why the government say if this has been the generally accepted practice in public bodies in this country, then it would be difficult for this parliament to upset that practice at the present time.
I may say that I think we would have been wiser in 1945-looking back now to those days-to have increased the indemnity somewhat then and made the whole amount taxable. But we did not do that. We set a precedent; we changed the Income Tax Act, and the result is that all the legislatures and many of the municipal bodies followed suit and made part of their emoluments tax-free.
When the bill is in committee, at the proper stage, I shall try to put our ideas in this particular on the record, that the indemnity should be $6,000 plus the $2,000 expense allowance. That is what most of my colleagues think should be the solution.
I turn now to the other factors and other proposals in the resolution. I shall say this. I said it in the house once before when the residence of the prime minister was under discussion some few years ago. Regardless of the personality of the prime minister- that is not the point; the point is the position of the prime minister in this country-I think most of us feel that the emoluments of the prime minister of this country certainly should not be very much less than the emoluments of the governor of the Bank of Canada or of the president of the Canadian National Railways. If the Prime Minister's emoluments are increased now they will still be considerably less than the emoluments of the two gentlemen whom I have just named.
Of course the same considerations may apply-we have some reservations regarding this-to the ministers of the crown who surround the Prime Minister; but there is one thing we cannot approve because of the position we take regarding it. We cannot approve the proposal to increase the indemnities of the hon. gentlemen who occupy seats in the other place. We believe that today this branch of the parliamentary institution-and I will not quote the words of Shelley regarding an unreformed senate; I suppose it would not be parliamentary if I did-is archaic and unrepresentative of the country. I say we cannot support that part of the Prime Minister's proposals because we view the other place in the manner in which I have just indicated. As long as the Senate is there I am not going to say anything against the senators, because I think many of them are very fine people.

Senate and House of Commons But it is an institution, unrepresentative, archaic, out-of-date, beyond the House of Lords in the powers that it now has.
A word with regard to the payment of the indemnities. All of us approve the method suggested by the Prime Minister of paying this on a 12-month basis. As to the dating of it, there may be some differences of opinion; but certainly it puts us on the basis of having no additional indemnities if parliament is called twice or indeed three times a year, and I think that is a very good thing. I never liked the two sessions. The Prime Minister may recall that on one occasion I objected to the possibility of it privately to him, but this obviates any misunderstanding that could occur across the country regarding the payment for two sessions, and that is an excellent feature of the proposals now before us.
Since the annual basis is desirable, it is desirable that the amount shall be paid in equal instalments, month by month, and paid from one election to the other. On the basis of the indemnity payable for 12 months no additional payment is possible by this house other than on a 12-month basis.
These are the principal points that I wanted to lay before the committee as the point of view of most of my colleagues of this party. Like the Prime Minister, we have considered this and we have come to conclusions in our own minds. I have placed before the committee what is the consensus of the largest group in our party regarding this very important matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have listened to the previous speakers with a good deal of interest. Before going into a general discussion of the subject may I deal with one or two things the Leader of the Opposition has said, and also one or two things the leader of the C.C.P. party has said.
In the first place, may I say that I agree with the Prime Minister and others that this is not a party matter; it is a matter that parliament as a whole must decide, and upon which each individual member must express himself. The Leader of the Opposition has recommended a royal commission, which does not strike my fancy at all; in the first place, because it does seem to me that when anything of this or of almost any similar nature arises our Conservative friends always suggest a royal commission. If I have heard that royal commission argument once over the past number of years I must have heard it a dozen times. My colleague the hon. member for Wetaskiwin whispers in my ear that perhaps this is the way the Conservative party has of


solving the unemployment problem. If we went forward with all the commissions they recommend everybody would be on one.
After all, does this involve such tremendous investigation that it requires a royal commission? There are perhaps a couple of dozen salaries involved. What is involved with respect to the increase in indemnities will vary, I suppose, from about $7,000 to $12,000, but surely it would not need a royal commission to decide that. I do not think the point is well taken.
I have not consulted with all my colleagues, but I think we are in favour of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in respect to the Senate. I am one who believes in the Senate. I think the Senate can be made to perform exceptionally useful functions, but there is one thing to be considered in respect to allowances for those in the other place. After all, they do not sit quite as long as we do. They do have periods of time when they can go back home and look after their businesses. On the other hand, when a session is not being held they do not have constituencies to look after. We do, and in recent years we have found that our job has become a fulltime job.
Then with respect to the resolution itself, I believe the country has been given some considerable notice that this resolution was expected. I am not familiar with the words of the Prime Minister in Vancouver referred to by the Leader of the Opposition, but the press have carried various dispatches referring to this particular measure. During that time the public and the press have had considerable time to comment on the matter. Except in a few cases the editorial comments I have read have pretty well been in favour of something of this kind. I have read some criticism in respect to increases for the Senate, and in respect to tax-free expense allowances, but generally speaking the press have favoured some such move as this.
As far as actual protests from the people are concerned, I can go only by the number of protests I have received. I will tell the house how many I have received-three letters. One of them was really bad. It called me everything under the sun. I turned to my secretary and said, "That fellow is a stinker." She said, "You had better be careful. It may not be a fellow; it may be a woman." The letter was not signed. However, it was not from anybody in my constituency so I did not worry very much about it.
The other letter contained a modified protest, and the writer was quite gentlemanly in his manner of writing his letter. I was

somewhat disturbed about the third letter, which came from a war veteran who was on the old age pension and receiving $20 per month by way of war veterans allowance. He wrote and said, "I am glad you are getting an increase, as I think you members of parliament are doing a pretty good job, but I do wish they would increase the war veterans allowance."
I should like to comment on that, because I fancy that the general belief among a lot of people whose incomes are very small would be something like this. Here are these members who have authority to increase their indemnities, yet we have to live on a shoestring. The psychology is bad. I do feel for them, but even though this measure were not introduced I am sure it would not mean an increase in such social services as old age pensions, war veterans allowances and the like. Of course it would not mean that.
Social services in this country run into a tremendously high figure, millions upon millions of dollars. I am sure if members of parliament were given a choice of having their allowances increased or of having an increase in social services such as old age pensions, war veterans allowances and the like, every hon. member would say, "By all means increase the old age pensions and war veterans allowances." Every one of us would do that. However, there is little relationship between the amount of money involved in this, even though it may sound like a lot, and the amount involved in increasing old age pensions, allowances and so forth by $10 or $15 a month.
There is another point which has been covered already. For the most part incomes have been practically doubled all along the line during the past number of years while our indemnities have remained the same. However, there is a feeling abroad which has been indicated in some of the editorials I have read, that while it is true others have received increases in salaries, wages and so forth, members of parliament have the power to increase their indemnities and as a result get it out of the taxpayer.
There is a misconception there. Those people do not realize when they say that, even editorially, that we are all taxpayers in one form or another. When the levels of salaries and wages are raised throughout the country it is written into the cost of production. A higher cost of living must come out of the taxpayers. The only difference is that it is not obtained through the income tax channel. It comes out of the baby's milk bottle, or out of the shoes and clothes we buy for our children. We are all taxpayers and it comes out of the taxpayer
Senate and House of Commons just as much as these other things do, though through a slightly different channel. I wish those who comment on these things would first make certain they have the proper picture.
There is another point that has not been considered, and that is that after all the government, which means the Canadian people or the national treasury of the country, is going to get back a pretty good slice of this in income tax. When people look at the Prime Minister's salary of, for instance, $25,000 they whistle and say, "My goodness, that is quite a chunk". Well, it is quite a chunk. I do not know how much it costs the Prime Minister to live, but even supposing it cost him $10,000-I happen to have some tax tables here-on that extra $15,000 he will pay over $5,000 in income tax. Therefore he does not get that $25,000. The same comparison can be applied relatively to the other cabinet ministers, and it applies relatively to us too.
I figured out my own income tax, and on the proposed increase I am going to pay a couple of thousand dollars. That is never considered when editorial comment is written. People see only the bold figures, forgetting that the government is going to get something back.
There is another point I would like to bring to the attention of the house, and particularly to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue. A great deal of editorial comment-I know I keep using that particular phrase, but after all if we want to get the opinion of the country we usually read the papers-stresses the fact that we get a $2,000 expense allowance tax free, and it is claimed we are the only ones in the country who get a tax-free allowance. But that is not true.

Every commercial traveller, anyone who goes out as an employee of a company, has an expense account on which he lives when he is away from home. While we are in committee I would like the Minister of National Revenue to offset that opinion by telling us what categories of

Senate and House of Commons expense allowances are similar to ours and therefore tax free. I think the information would surprise the country. In fact I think it would be advisable if he did give the house that information.

I spoke at a public meeting during the Christmas recess, and at that meeting there were gathered some farmers and labour men. I knew what was in that gentleman's mind because I knew him and he was no supporter of mine. So I said to him: "I do not know. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
This is one of these matters which come before parliament which impose a tremendous responsibility on each and every member of the House of Commons. That was stated by the Prime Minister in his opening remarks. It is in that spirit that I rise to support the suggestion made by my leader, the Leader of the Opposition, that parliament and the country have not sufficient information upon which to act, as parliament is arbitrarily asked to act under the terms of this resolution.
Only the other day I was reading the works of the French philosopher Diderot. That philosopher said that when the artist thinks of money, he loses his sense of beauty. I think those words apply with particular force when we debate a question such as this affecting, as it does, the democratic rights in our country and the need for maintaining parliament in its amplitude so that it may truly represent and lead the Canadian people.
Someone said that a royal commission would shift responsibility. It would do nothing of the sort. Is the government shifting responsibility when it asks for the setting up of a royal commission in connection with 83276-93
Senate and House o} Commons the criminal law, in order to deal with certain amendments to be made to the Criminal Code? Nothing of the kind. I hope that is not shifting responsibility. The other day the Minister of Justice announced that a royal commission would be set up in order to secure the opinions of people generally qualified to speak with regard to certain changes to be made in the law.
Above everything else, as we discuss this matter, we dare not allow the Canadian people to come to the conclusion that parliament, because we have the power here, can become a grab-bag at the option of any of us or all of us. I believe that a royal commission would go far to enable the people of Canada and parliament to learn the facts. Certainly the Prime Minister has placed before parliament no reason why some of the increases to which reference has been made should, in fact, be made or why the figure fixed in this resolution as the increase for members of both houses of parliament should indeed be the proper figure.
The Prime Minister endeavoured to answer the possible charge that this matter was left until after the election before action was taken by parliament. On July 9 he made a radio speech which, as I heard it, gave no indication to the Canadian people that, in the first session after the election, there was to be an increase in the indemnities. We who were elected-we were not conscripted to be candidates-were elected on the basis that the indemnities we were to receive were, in fact, the ones we had been receiving. I find it difficult to understand why this measure, if it is so necessary, should have been introduced now, immediately after an election. I find it difficult to understand why it should not have been introduced last session, to be implemented after the election. In 1920, when an increase took place, it was within a few months of the expected date of the election.
One thing further I should like the Prime Minister to explain is this. If this increase is necessary, or if it is required to be made, why should it be made retroactive to November 12, the beginning of the present session? What is the reason for that?

I believe the people of Canada are not in favour of this measure as now constituted. At a time like this I think the people of Canada are asking the members of this chamber to practise a degree of selfcontrol that is not apparent when a measure such as this is brought forward with such haste for the purpose of putting it through in the same manner.
