speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am only going to say a very few words at this stage of the debate, largely to indicate where I stand with regard to this question. As the Prime Minister was explaining the purpose of the resolution to the committee I was struck by the thought that he must have been a very effective lawyer in court. As a matter of fact, as he explained the difficulties and hardships of members of parliament I began to feel that I had suffered quite considerably in the public interest during the last 24 years. I was afraid there was something hypnotic about his words, and I closed my eyes and began to make a rough calculation of the years of my life.
I was brought up on a farm, and on a farm you go to work pretty early in life. I have put down ten years of age as the time when I really began to work, but I am quite sure I was doing my share of the work long before that. But after that time I really worked. There was no time for school, no time for university, no time for anything except work and bearing the responsibility for running the family farm after the head of the family had passed away. From the time I was ten until I entered the House of Commons I found that there was a period of about 35 years, and I thought of the various kinds of work I did during that space of time.
I must say that I have never had it so easy as since I became a member of parliament. I do not think I have neglected my work as a member of parliament. When your home is in Vancouver you cannot go home very often on these Thursday to Tuesday week ends, and whether or not I wanted to I had to stay here. As I had to stay here I of course was working. I was on the job-seven days a week. Between sessions I was helping to build a new party, and there is

no part of the country with the exception of the province of Newfoundland, where I have not spoken and spent considerable time.
When I am at home people are continually coming to me about little matters. Nevertheless I must state, as I siaid before, that I have never had it as soft as since I came here. I believe that is true of members of parliament in general. I noted what the Leader of the Opposition said about the difficulty in finding members to serve in the other place, but even as far as the House of Commons is concerned there is no great difficulty in getting candidates.
I look across the floor and I see people who have stood for office election after election. They feel they are lucky if they are elected. New members come here, and there is a general scramble to get a seat in this house. We come here not because of the indemnity, salary, or whatever you want to call it. I must say it is go:ng to come pretty close to a salary if the indemnity is to be put on a monthly basis. We come here because we like the work and associations, and feel that this is where we wiant to be.
The hon. member for Macleod said that a lawyer who would come here for $6,000 a year must be somewhat of a two-by-four lawyer in his own community. I can look around the chamber and see members who are not two-by-four lawyers either in their own or any other community. If we are going to make the size of the indemnity the reason members come here, we are not going to raise the standards of this house; we are going to lower them. The Leader of the Opposition made some reference to reasonable or satisfactory-I do not know exactly the words he used-compensation for the sacrifices made. Surely the hon. member knows that you cannot be paid for sacrifices. A sacrifice is something you make because you want to do it. If you are to be paid for it, it is not a sacrifice.
My main objection to this increase-I am not going into the figures now-is that it increases the spread between members of parliament and members of the government and the people we govern. If there is anything that history shows us has caused trouble down through the ages, it has been the economic separation of the people from the government. This has caused a great deal of the world's troubles. Every time we raise the salaries of cabinet ministers or the indemnities of members of parliament, without at the same time raising the incomes of the people in our community who need to have their incomes raised, we are separating our 83276-931
Senate and House of Commons government from the people. That is a bad thing for any country.
I said when I began that I was not going to say much. If I do not stop soon I shall not be holding to that statement. I am opposed to this measure, first of all because of the amount of increase. I believe it is fantastic. I did not hear anyone say, throughout the whole of the election campaign, that he or she was going to Ottawa for the purpose of raising his or her indemnity at the first opportunity. From no party, Liberal, Conservative, C.C.F. or Social Credit, have I heard any suggestion that this was the first thing they were going to do. Every member I heard speak from the public platform, every member I saw reported in the newspapers, every member I heard over the radio, said he was coming here for the purpose of improving the conditions of those amongst us whose conditions need to be improved. Reference was made to old age pensioners, persons on war veterans allowance, and many on low incomes who, as one newspaper stated editorially not so long ago, never have enough to eat. This situation exists in this rich country to which the Prime Minister referred.
I, amongst others, said I was coming down here, and asked my people to send me down here, to do something for those who were unable to do something for themselves, and for those who could not come here and raise their own incomes. I am not going to support any increase in income for any member of parliament until we have made some attempt at raising the incomes of the poor in this rich country.

Mr. Chairman, I was saying that there are everywhere in Canada old people who cannot, on $40 a month, live and meet their obligations, pay their rent, eat properly and dress decently. A great number of these old people, all across the country, are asking the government to increase their pension. We turn down their legitimate request, and yet at the same time, we members of parliament are going to vote ourselves a 100 per cent increase!
I have before me the correspondence I received today; these 151 letters have come to me from people of the working class, men with large families, who have been asking for a long time, on account of the steady increase of the cost of living and the overburden of taxation, an increase in family allowances in order to be able to meet their obligations and give a little more happiness to their families. Do you think that in the face of such a legitimate request I would feel happy to meet these


people and tell them that while their request has been turned down, we have been pleased to support the Prime Minister's motion to double our indemnity.
There are at present all across Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, young people, single or married, who during the last world war gave their best for the defence of Canada, their motherland.
A large number of them-and the hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) could surely corroborate this-write in every day to ask whether it would not be possible to increase the pittance which they receive since it is not sufficient to enable them to meet their obligations. And yet, while these people who have risked their life for Canada are refused the pension which they are asking for we are expected to be so inconsistent as to support this motion now before us and to increase our indemnities 100 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, in the past year, every important public body in this country has been urging a reduction in income tax. There is nothing to indicate though that in his next budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will bring this about. All important public bodies in this country are therefore being refused a fair request. No small increase in pensions or family allowances is being granted those who are really in need of it and yet, at the very same time, the right hon. the Prime Minister, who himself represents a district almost wholly made up of working people, is asking us to support this resolution and, as servants of the people, to vote ourselves this 100 per cent increase.
I believe this measure to be highly unpopular at the present time. The government will be the one to answer for it to the taxpayers of this country.
In spite of the statements made in and out of this house by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) and other cabinet members, there is at this time an economic recession in the offing. Thousands of workers are out of work. They are asking for employment, they are urging the government to proceed with public works so as to be in a position at least to earn a living for themselves, their wives and children. The government have done nothing to alleviate their plight.
Where can you find logic in this resolution moved by the right hon. the Prime Minister? I would have liked him to have had the opportunity, before introducing this resolution in the house, to visit his constituency, to make a tour of all the little streets in St. Roch and

St. Jean Baptiste districts. He would have seen that all these workers are sitting at home, waiting for some help to provide for their families. Had he done so, I wonder if he would have come before us today with this same resolution which he has just introduced to the members of the house.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me absolutely contrary to the principles of sound democracy to adopt this resolution as worded. I rather think it should have been submitted to the people, even before the election of August last. If only the hon. members opposite had adopted in front of the people, in front of their electors, the arrogant attitude which they are now displaying in the house toward those who do not share their opinions, I bet there would not be 50 per cent of them who would now be sitting on that side of the house this year.
We must, of course, think of the people before looking after those who claim to be their servants. When one wants to serve, one is called upon to make sacrifices; if one is not ready to make the sacrifices required of us as representatives of the people, there is only one thing to do: it is to refuse to stand for election when we are requested to do so. I shall perhaps be reminded that respect is due to the properly constituted authority. I agree with that, but if this authority which is constituted by the people for the people fails to look after the real and urgent needs of the people, here is what is going to happen. We shall have to go through the same deplorable situation now prevalent in various iron curtain countries; and we shall have to fight, even more firmly, against communism at home. If we do not want communism in this country, let us not pass resolutions which would only embitter certain people.
I believe that the motion is untimely and I very simply wish to dissociate myself from the responsibility which the government would like us to assume. Moreover, I want the country to know and especially the electors of my riding that I am against this resolution because instead of thinking of myself I want to think of those who elected me, their wives and children, who are at present in need.
I think that those few words will reflect the feelings of all my constituents and I hope that the Prime Minister will study carefully those few remarks and reconsider

Mr. Chairman, I suppose it is inevitable that in the discussion of any proposal which involves consideration of the indemnities to be paid to members of parliament it should be a little bit embarrassing for any one of us who is actually a member to take part, because however much we may try to put it upon the plane that we are setting a level of indemnities which will preserve the dignity of and respect for parliament as an institution, the fact remains that we are nevertheless discussing what will be the level of remuneration for our own services.
Furthermore, in dealing with this matter we are in a position enjoyed by no other people in the country; we are in a position, whatever may be our decision, to vote upon it and increase the level of our remuneration at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada, a body of which, it must be admitted-and I am frank to admit it-we ourselves are also all members. But there is no one else in the country in that position; therefore it is a subject which is always a little difficult to discuss.


I do not think there is any need for any of us to hesitate to agree that there is certainly a case for some increase in the indemnities, and for the argument that the level now paid requires revision. But I for one am certainly not prepared to swallow, without discussion, the figure which is put forward by the government and which will be introduced in legislation if this resolution carries.
In discussion of matters of this sort, both here and at home with my friends, when sometimes it has been suggested that we must be foolish to be members at the present level of indemnity and so on and that we should vote ourselves increases, it has always seemed to me that we should not lose sight of the fact that we are all free, white and 21, and that no one held a pistol to the head of any one of us and said, "You have to run for parliament; you have to accept nomination and run for election". In fact in my constituency in 1949 there were three others who contested the seat and in 1953 there were also three others, all of them estimable gentlemen, any one of whom would have been delighted to come down here instead of me. We all ran on the basis of the present indemnity.
I therefore do not think one can take as a sufficient argument to support this resolution to give us this increase in indemnity that you cannot get candidates unless you accept the present proposal. I always remind myself of those other two occasions when three other gentlemen would have been extremely glad to come down here for the present indemnity if I myself had not run and been successful.
In laying the basis for a discussion of a proposal which involves an increase in indemnities, it seems to me that one should perhaps try to sort out one's thinking on why we become members of parliament, and one's thinking on the motives and on the standards for membership. It seems to me, as it has always seemed, that there are three chief considerations in the mind of anyone who offers himself for public service as a member of the House of Commons of Canada. The one which I would put first and most important is the desire to give public service. That consideration, it seems to me, is and must always be the paramount motive. I would put second the very proper desire for power; that is to say, the desire to have a say in the conduct of the affairs of the nation. I do not suppose any one of us would have offered himself for election and been anxious to come down here unless he felt that he had

a contribution to make. That is what I call- and it may not be an apt phrase-the proper desire tor power, or the desire to place yourself in a position where you can influence the conduct of national affairs. I would put third -and only third, after those other two motives-the financial considerations which may enter into the picture.
That being my view of the matter, I say for myself, at any rate, that I think we must be careful not to approach the subject from the point of view that the financial remuneration to a member must be such that there shall never be any element of sacrifice, because I do not think that is a sound starting point for such a discussion.
Having made those general observations, I should like to turn to a particular consideration of the resolution before us and of the discussion which has taken place so far today. As will be recalled, it has been suggested by the Leader of the Opposition, that this matter should not now be put forward for the decision of the house but rather that a royal commission should be appointed to study and report upon it so that, with the benefit of their investigation, we might be in a position to make a decision which would perhaps be a more impartial one than we are in a position to make at the present time. I am fully in accord with that suggestion.
We have already heard from other hon. members on all sides that use is being made of the same old tactics-as they say-of saying that we are doing the right thing but that we are doing it by the wrong method. Mr. Chairman, I think this matter goes a great deal further than that. I do not think it is doing the right thing to try to put this proposal through in its present form without the benefit of such a previous study. I think it is doing the wrong thing, not doing the right thing in the wrong way. I think it is the wrong thing to do in this way., for a number of reasons.
The first reason is this. There was no announcement to the people, prior to the election, that an increase in indemnities to members and senators, in the salaries of ministers and of leaders of the opposition, would be put through, when the opportunity was available to the Prime Minister and the government party to make the statement prior to the election.
I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that prior to the increase put through in 1945 it was, in effect, stated by the then prime minister-indeed, I think it was stated in so many words-that, if returned, he would 83276-94
Senate and House of Commons regard it as a mandate to provide an increase in the remuneration of members of parliament. That issue was clearly before the people. I therefore think there could have been no objection to the method followed in 1945, in view of the statement made by the then prime minister during the course of the election campaign. No such statement was made on this occasion. No hint was given to the people of Canada that, if returned, this government would put through, at the first session, such a substantial increase in indemnities to members of the House of Commons and of the Senate, as well as the other increases which are now before us.

I quite agree with him. This applies with equal force to both members and senators. I rest my case also on the larger ground that when we consider the advisability of amending the act it is quite in order to suggest that there are other respects in which it requires amendment. Speaking for myself, I say without any hesitation that I believe the act should be amended to make it impossible for ministers to hold directorships in corporations having dealings with government departments.
These are all matters, you see, on which it is difficult for private members or members of the government to hold impartial views. In that respect, I believe a study of the matter by a royal commission would be beneficial because such a commission could say whether the moral principles, if I may call them that, which gave rise to the provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act are applicable today, or whether they should be relaxed or tightened. I just do not think it is good enough for us to take the high moral position that the reason for increasing the indemnity is to enable us to preserve complete independence and objectivity in dealing with public business, if we are not prepared to consider also that act which lays down the code of conduct of members of the parliament.
Then I believe, too, that the question of whether or not the Senate and House of Commons Act should be tightened up with respect to the arrangements made for members receiving these indemnities should be studied by a royal commission. If this bill becomes law, we are going to be placed in the position of receiving a substantial sum of money. In anyone's language $10,000 is a lot of money. In so far as we can, I think we should place ourselves in a position above reproach in respect of the receipt of that money, and indeed with respect to the receipt of our indemnity whatever it may be.

a person to receive the indemnity, whatever it may be, he must in fact devote that attention to the business of the nation which the rules and regulations set out. It is my own view that the act itself, and the regulations in that regard, are in need of substantial overhauling.

Mr. Chairman, it is perhaps
unfortunate that I did not take more time to prepare an address for the purpose of this particular debate. It would, of course, only be necessary for me to jot down a few notes. Since I have been here-and I came in 1949-I think there has been before this house no legislation with whose aspects I am more familiar. This is one piece of legislation as to which I do not need guidance by a royal commission. I do not need a royal commission to tell me whether or not I feel that I should, in conscience, vote for an increase in the indemnity of members of parliament.
It has been said that, in taking cognizance of this legislation, a member should not be swayed by his own personal views. However, I fail to see how it would be possible for any member to vote intelligently on this question unless he gave some consideration to how it affects him-because, after all, he is the member of parliament-and the public in general. Anyone we might appoint to a royal commission would not be familiar with the various expenses of a member, the various things to which a member of parliament is expected to contribute, or just how his affairs need to be handled.
I wonder how a royal commission would proceed. Would a royal commission inquire as to the standard of living of the various members of parliament, as to what they live in when they come to Ottawa, what their occupations are at home, what they live in before coming here and so on? Just how would they determine whether a member needs additional income?
The strange thing about this matter is this. The first time I heard the matter broached in the House of Commons was by a Conservative member who, I am led to believe, is not exactly a poor man. I refer to the hon. member for Simcoe North. That was some two years ago. That is only a remark by the way, but it is an indication. For my part, I know that for the last several years the matter has been discussed amongst members and parties, in the hope that there was a general intention of making life here as a member of parliament more amicable. It is for that reason I am quite confident that it did not come as a surprise to any member of the opposition that this question would be raised following the general election of last year.
If we were to get down to cases-and I do not think it should be necessary-and if we were to consider the hours of work, for instance, as I have done as a union officer when we were making representations before management, I might point out that most
Senate and House of Commons members of parliament arrive at their offices here between nine and ten o'clock in the morning. It is seldom that they leave before the hour of ten; and until the last parliament, I believe it was, they remained in the building until eleven o'clock at night. That means a 14-hour day with, of course, time off for lunch and so forth; but they are more or less on duty that full time. Apart from the hours, I do not want to go into the matter of actual pay for work done, because that was not my intention when I came to this house. On that basis alone I believe there is some justification for doing something about increasing the indemnity.
I have travelled considerably with union officers who represent the people in another sphere than as members of the House of Commons. Very few of these people, and rightly so, are paid less than $6,000 a year. As happened in my own case when I was a union representative, from the time a union officer steps into a taxi at the door of his house when proceeding on any type of union work until the time he gets home he is paid his expenses. That amounts to quite a large sum of money. When a member of parliament reaches his home after leaving the house at the end of a session it is necessary for him to travel much more than a union officer, but he does so at his own expense.
In saying this, I do not want my constituents to feel that they are taking advantage of me when they ask me to go here and there throughout my riding, but I simply wish to point out that every time you step into an automobile these days and drive a few hundred miles it runs into quite a large amount of money. Those are some of the reasons I think the work we do and the amount of time we spend on it justify more than $6,000 a year.
I might mention in passing that quite a number of miners in Canada made around $6,000 last year. It is true that their work is much more arduous, but they are living at home and their expenses are certainly not commensurate with those of a member of parliament. I do not think they want their members of parliament to live in any poorer circumstances than those in which they are able to live.
Certainly when one is discussing these things one has his own personal situation to consider. So far as a young man with a family is concerned, a semi-monkish existence is no existence for him at all. It is not a good thing for him to have his family in the far west, to live here and have to maintain two homes, and it certainly is an expensive arrangement. If such a member moves his

Senate and House of Commons family here he runs into much more expense than is involved in living at home. No matter how you look at it there is considerable sacrifice, and unless a man is willing to live in a garret and put up with much poorer conditions than in his own home he cannot expect to carry on.
A number of hon. members on the opposition side have made reference to the fact that considerable time is spent by some members away from the house, that there is some absenteeism and so on. I think it would be unfair to point to any one member or group of members, but it may be that those with professional practices in their ridings are in a much better position financially than those of us who have to work in mines or factories, and they might be inclined to be absent from the house more than those who do not have these businesses.
I thought the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre repudiated his own people this afternoon in a manner which I would not think would be acceptable to them. My contention has always been that a member should maintain connections with his own riding and that he should not become a professional politician. I am quite confident that any young married man attempting to raise and educate a family and having to move them back and forth across this continent will not become a professional politician for the sum of $10,000. The amount will have to be considerably more before such a man will be induced to become what the hon. member has called a professional politician.
But I do believe there are some in the C.C.F. ranks who make a calling of being a member of parliament, and I am sure that if they do they should not be called professional politicians. They are making a very great sacrifice, and I certainly think they deserve all the credit we can give them. But I cannot see how they can maintain and educate a family, and look forward to further education of their families, on $6,000 a year as members of parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to talk out this measure, but I have a few words to say on it. As will be indicated when the vote is taken, and as has been suggested so far by the speeches made by members of this group, we are completely democratic. We are split three ways, which indicates that members of our group are completely free. As far as I am concerned, I want to say that the Prime Minister in introducing this measure is making an honest attempt to solve a problem that has existed for some considerable time. I do not think anyone can accuse


him of having any personal motives. This will probably be his last term, and to my mind he fits pretty well a definition I have seen, namely that a politician thinks in terms of elections and a statesman thinks in terms of the future generation. He is laying the groundwork for his successor.
I think it is incorrect to say that this measure requires more study, that it has not been thought of, and that it comes as a surprise. I have heard it talked about in the corridors for the past four years. I have heard it debated in the cafeteria and I have heard it psychoanalysed in the parliamentary restaurant. Therefore I do not think anyone is fooled when someone tries to kid us that we do not know one another's opinions about this matter, because we do.
With respect to the idea of a royal commission, I think the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar was absolutely correct when he said that it was an attempt to shift responsibility. Royal commissions are not new things. The people in the part of the country from which I come look upon royal commissions with a great deal of suspicion, because they recall that in the past we have attempted to solve all the problems of this country by means of royal commissions. These commission reports never accomplished anything except to gather dust in the archives. The hon. member for Temiscouata is quite right when he says the commission would likely be composed of members of the judiciary. They would be barred from membership in the commission on a ground which the hon. member did not mention. They would be dealing with a matter in which they were personally concerned, because we establish their salaries and if they did not pass substantial increases for us they might not get their own salaries increased. We would have to go to some other profession to get a commission to handle this problem.
A commission was established in the United States, and hon. members are familiar with what happened there. No doubt that commission was composed of jurists, but despite the salaries which congressmen are getting the commission recommended a 100 per cent increase. You see, the members of the judiciary have rather lucrative salaries, and live rather well. They may set standards for us which are too high. There is no solution there.
Someone suggested a poll of public opinion across this country. A poll of public opinion was taken in the United States. People with good salaries and with poor salaries were canvassed. I have seen the results of that poll; as a matter of fact I have them here.

The housewife and the chap with a small millinery shop, the people with poor salaries and substantial salaries, all were canvassed, and there was not one person in that group who said the net income of a member of congress, after taxes, should be less than $20,000 per year. Many of them said it should be .$25,000.
The two suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition are not workable here. They were tried in the United States, and the opinion was that the top executives of the country, the people who pass the laws and who have the power to declare wars, to requisition your boy or girl for service, and who have to take that responsibility, were entitled to a great deal more remuneration than they are receiving now.
I am a strong believer in equal pay for equal work. If you are going to measure from that standard-and I firmly believe that is the standard that should be used-our opposite number, the congressman in the United States, receives a higher indemnity than we do. It is the philosophy of the union movement across this country to try to raise our standards to those of the United States worker for comparable work. I think we are in good company when we take that position in this house. I feel that I am worth as much, I feel every member in this house is worth as much, as the congressmen in the United States. We shall not reach their position in one jump, but it is a goal for which we should strive. I do not believe in pulling down the standards.
There has been a reference to the War Veterans Allowance Act. I know all about that act because I had the privilege of helping to write the first draft of it some time ago. I have followed its course ever since, trying to shove the allowance up as high as I could. Hon. members who use the recipients of old age pensions and war veterans allowances as an argument here are using an argument which does not belong here. I believe the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre said that the amount involved in this proposal might be $1-5 million. If you take that money and apply it to the old age pension or the war veterans allowance and other social legislation in this country, it will not mean anything by way of increase. It certainly is not an argument that can be used here.
The people in the part of the country from which I come will not need explanations about this measure. A good many times in the past they have asked me what was the matter with members of parliament. We went through a war with a $4,000 indemnity
Senate and House of Commons which was taxed to the hilt. We had no expense allowance, and were the only people in Canada who had to spend about half of our income in earning our income, and who did not have a tax offset for that expense. Some of my people used to ask me what was the matter with the fellows up here. They said, "How can we expect you to do something for us when you will not do something for yourselves?" They thought we were carrying a load which we should not be carrying, and that we should go after some exemptions.
I have no hesitation in saying that I see this measure as introduced by the Prime Minister as a start on something I have been thinking about for many years. Before I came to the House of Commons I viewed it as a rich man's club; but unless you had sufficient income to look after your family for 12 months you just could not afford to take a vacation for two and a half months and live on the indemnity that was paid at that time.
In my opinion the indemnity was designed at that time to be used for the purpose of keeping people out of this forum who were not in a financial position to support themselves and take a vacation until the next election came along. The main criticism in my part of the country has been that you see a member when he is seeking election, but for the remainder of the four years you never see him. When I accepted the nomination, I want to say that I did not seek it. I did not want it, and I nominated someone else at the convention and made a speech for him. The convention said that I could not decline. We ballot and if you are the nominee, you are it.

They do not want him to live in cheap rooming houses. They want him to be on a par with other executives in other organizations across the country. The average member who is trying to make this as nearly as possible a full-time job has not been in a financial position to do so for the last 12 or 14 years.
You can take the argument of cheapening things and discuss other emoluments that are lower. The school of thought I was brought up in does not think in that way. Take, for example, the position of the wage earner in this country today. Our wages are pretty high in comparison with India, Africa, Japan and other countries that we are going to have trouble with in the future in matters of trade. But the trade union movement of this country are not taking the position that they are going to lower their standards in order to compete with the low wages of those countries I have mentioned. They are organizing themselves, and they are sending men out to India, Africa, China and Japan to organize the workers, to lift the standards in those countries so they will not pull us down because of underselling us in world markets or even coming into our own country in the future.
That is the principle that is involved here. As far as I am concerned, all the money I get here enables me to do more work in this field in which I am engaged. I consider it is missionary work; I consider it is educational work; I believe that we have to get out and around, to keep in touch with our people. We are living in an uncertain world. We have to keep informed in order to do our work, and you must have ways and means of getting around.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to
oppose the resolution I want to say at the outset that I have only the highest possible respect for views which may be opposed to those I express, and which may be held by other hon. members. I believe that both the Prime Minister and the leader of our group were quite right when they said that
[Mr. Gillis.l

on a matter such as this each individual member should use his own best judgment rather than take it as a partisan matter. I am speaking, therefore, for myself, expressing my own personal views.
I have no hesitation in saying that I oppose this measure on the ground first of all that, in spite of what has been said here that there had been some hints or indications that something of this nature might be brought down after the election, I was neither informed, consulted, nor even heard the hint anywhere before August 10 that it wgs the intention of this government to bring a measure such as this before the house at this session.
I believe it is our duty to keep good faith with our electors. Had this matter been submitted to the electors of Canada previous to the election, and had the Prime Minister, when he made his radio broadcast to which he referred, in which he announced that he would press for or recommend certain changes in the rules of the house which might bring about greater efficiency, at the same time announced that the government intended to bring forth a measure to increase indemnities and salaries as contained in this resolution, then the people across Canada would have been informed and would have known of the intentions of the government. They could have discussed the matter in an open, democratic manner, as they have the habit of doing, with all the candidates in each of the ridings. I do not say they would have taken this stand or the other stand, because I do not think we know at the present time what the opinion of the people of Canada is on this issue which was not submitted to them for their consideration.
On that ground I would have to oppose the resolution, but there are other reasons. One of the reasons is that in the Prime Minister's address he made reference to the fact that the cost of living had risen rather substantially in recent years. I can remember so vividly how many times in this very house my colleagues warned the government in 1945, 1946 and years following, as did many other hon. members, that the actions they were taking or contemplating in abolishing the controls that we had-price controls-would result in a situation where there would have to be increases in salaries, wages and so forth, right across the board. The government did not heed those warnings. They brought on the situation themselves and, as a matter of fact, took a rather stubborn attitude on many occasions, as much as to say, "We do not need your advice; we know what we are doing." Now we are faced with this situation, and it is

still not clear-it may be made clear before this debate is finished-as to whose request is being carried out.
Upon whose request is this measure being introduced? The Prime Minister of course said quite properly that he and the government are prepared to take full responsibility. It is a government measure. But that is not the whole story. Certainly it was not the prime minister in council who simply got the bright idea and said, "Let us suggest to the house that we raise the indemnities by $4,000 and see how the boys take it".
It must have gone further than that. The request must have come from some responsible group of persons in this country. Was it the rank and file members of the Liberal party? If that were so I believe this house should be so informed. Then we would at least know where this thing originated. As it is now, it is something put before the house and the only justification given, that I can see, with any substance behind it is the fact that the cost of living has risen and we therefore must make some provision to see that the average member of parliament may continue to do his work.
If that argument holds good for the members of this house, and the members of the Senate, members of the government, the Leader of the Opposition and all others concerned, surely the cost of living has not fallen for the rank and file wage earners, farmers, and other people across this country. They have suffered just as much at the hands of the government's decontrol policy as have the individual members of this house. Then because we happen to be in the position- I speak collectively as a whole parliament now-where we are temporarily the custodians of the people's tax money, that does not excuse us nor does it excuse the government for neglecting all those other groups and not providing something for those who are not so close to the source of supply, unless you are willing to accept the old legal proverb that possession is nine-tenths of the law.
It has been suggested that this matter be submitted to a royal commission. Obviously I would not support that suggestion, though if I were on the other side of this question, if I were in favour of an increase, I would think there might be something to that proposal because there would be something to investigate. But since I am not supporting the measure I obviously see no reasons for submitting anything to a royal commission. Our experience with royal commissions has been such that it appears to me the end result if we submitted this question to a royal commission
Senate and House of Commons would be that instead of adding a burden of $1,500,000 to the taxpayers we would be adding an extra $500,000 and making it $2 million, because royal commissions have to be paid also. Let us not forget that. They do not do their work for nothing. I see no reason why we should add cost upon cost.
I am speaking for myself when I say I am opposing this resolution. I repeat that I respect the views of all others who have spoken. It is quite clear that this is not a question as to whether we need an increase. It is not a question which can be decided by speaking of all the members of the house as a unit. We are not all in the same position. It is an academic question which could be debated for years. Sooner or later this parliament will decide, and naturally the majority view will have to be accepted and respected. But I shall make my stand perfectly clear, on the ground that this was not submitted to the electorate, nor was any opportunity given to us who participated in the election to submit it to our electors, or even consult with them or discuss it with them in any way. On that ground alone I find it impossible to give my support to this measure.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want simply to clear up one or two points which have been raised, in view of the fact that there has been an obvious attempt to obscure the issue that was presented. The question was not that there was any objection to rewarding or reimbursing members in keeping with their responsibilities. It was stated clearly several times and quite emphatically that in our belief the people of this country were quite prepared to provide from public funds an adequate return to members of parliament. But that does not deal with the other problems that are raised.
The resolution before us does not deal alone with members' allowances or indemnities. As I said before, it is a rolled-up package. Members are to vote on an increase for the members of the Senate, about whom not one word has been said by way of support, by way of argument or by way of evidence. They are increasing cabinet ministers' salaries and the salaries of the leaders of the opposition in this house and the Senate by $9,000, but not one word has been said as to why that should be done. When I say "by $9,000" I mean by the $4,000 they will receive as members and the $5,000 which will also be granted to members of the government. Not one word has been put forward to explain how that figure was arrived at. Where did it come from?

Senate and House of Commons
I repeat what I said this afternoon. This house has been told over and over again that we must be cautious about handling public funds. There are a number of matters about which the people of this country are pressing for action, and we are told that there must be a great deal of consideration before any commitments are made. It was my hope that by suggesting a royal commission we would provide a method of inquiry into this and the other matters raised by this motion which would not leave the suggestion that while we were insistent upon the last bit of evidence to support the needs of others who depend upon parliament, we were in great haste to pass legislation-and without evidence-that would bring benefits to members of parliament themselves. It is as simple as that.
Mr. Chairman, a great deal has been said about the suggestion of a royal commission. If the Prime Minister would say that he would agree to a select committee and throw it wide open, I would say that while I favour a royal commission I would not object to that method, which was the method employed at Westminster on the last occasion a change was made there and which has been employed on similar occasions here. I say that by one method or the other, by a royal commission or a select committee, we should be in position to obtain more evidence that we have now.
We have no information as to how these figures were arrived at that are now before us. What happens in regard to the pension? Unless there is legislation that is not disclosed, the pension will be increased by this procedure. Should there be no examination of that subject? Should there be no evidence as to the actuarial problems involved and what it will cost the public treasury if that is done? We are not accepting our responsibilities as members if we agree to support a resolution which says it is expedient that this legislation be introduced unless we have evidence before us to support that contention. That is our position.
When I suggested a royal commission it was not that I was wedded to that proposal. It was simply that I was asking that we have information which we should have. It is very interesting to hear hon. members on the opposite side speak in such contemptuous terms of royal commissions. One statement that was made was that all any royal commission has done is make a report which goes to the archives to gather dust.
Was that the purpose of the royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences? Was that simply a cynical waste of public money? Was that simply an attempt to send


something to the archives without any consideration? The royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences was set up under a distinguished Canadian to report on subjects of concern to Canadians. I have not heard previously the cynical suggestion that this was simply a device to avoid responsibility.
When it is suggested by the hon. member for Temiscouata that the appointment of a commission is only to avoid making a decision-

At least there are some of us who think those commissions did provide interesting and useful information, whether or not members of the house agreed with everything that was put forward. No matter whether we agree with all this government does or with the reports of commissions, we have not gone so far as to suggest that on every occasion they have appointed a royal commission it has been with the entirely cynical purpose of simply avoiding responsibility.
It was said tonight that it was uncertain where we stand. There is no uncertainty. We have stated that we believe there should be an increase in the indemnities and allowances paid to members, based upon inquiry which will give us some information as to how the figure is arrived at. But that is no reason why we should give a blank cheque for everything else contained in this proposal. Certainly it is no reason why we should agree in this motion that it is expedient that this legislation be introduced. We have heard nothing to support any of the measures contained therein, outside of the proposal to increase the indemnity of the members.
We have not heard any convincing argument as to the need for an increased indemnity to encourage men to come forward to become members of the other house. That is the reason we are told this should be done in this case. As far as this is concerned, we cannot call for a recorded vote. However, I certainly shall oppose this motion in committee in the absence of any assurance that there

is going to be an opportunity to obtain the information we should have. Certainly at the time this bill comes before us, if this resolution is passed, there will be an opportunity to deal with it in the ordinary way and register our objection in a more formal manner.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, after all we are here for the purpose of getting evidence and hearing facts. What about the question of the pension? Is that legislation going to be amended so that a double pension as compared to what we are receiving today will not be paid? Surely the Prime Minister is going to give some information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister is not going to make any commitments on this resolution. If it is not good enough on its merits, it should not carry.
With respect to pensions, if the hon. gentleman wishes to have the committee that considered the matter before consider what the actuarial implications will be, there can be no objection to having that matter go to the committee to have it report back to this house what information it can get in that regard.
With respect to these other matters, I am not going to make any commitment. The resolution itself merely refers to the expediency of introducing bills to increase these indemnities. The figures are not set out in the resolution. The figures will be set out in the bills. I told the house what was going to be recommended in the bills, but in debating this resolution the house is not debating the bill. The bills have to be considered and have three readings, and there will be ample opportunity then to discuss the details of the bills and obtain all the information that can be made available on the figures that will be contained in the bills. The resolution merely states:
That it is expedient to introduce measures to amend (a) the Senate and House of Commons Act to increase the salaries of the Speakers and the Deputy Speaker, the sessional allowances of members of the Senate and of the House of Commons ...
And:
(b) the Salaries Act to increase the salaries of ministers mentioned . . .
And so on. There are no details in the resolution, which merely refers to the advisability of introducing amending legislation to deal with these matters. The position then is that if the resolution is adopted the bills will be introduced, they will be distributed, and they can be fully discussed in all their particulars.

The hon. gentleman
knows that that pension act was put before the house, and that it is subject to re-examination at each and every session. The government will have no objection to having it reconsidered by the banking and commerce committee and to an actuarial investigation to determine what the effect will be. When the act was introduced it was not intended that it should be any more onerous on the treasury than the obligation of equalizing the contributions made to the fund by the members of parliament themselves. It was expected, on the information we got from the actuary, that the fund would be ample to provide the pensions that are called for by the terms of the act, and the government would wish at all times to have that carefully checked because it is not intended to make that a greater charge upon the treasury than was intended at the time, namely to equalize the contributions made by the members themselves.

It is all very well to say the government would have no objection to the matter being referred to the banking and commerce committee. The Prime Minister knows; you, sir, know; every member of this committee and every member of the house knows that if the government does not introduce legislation to amend the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act then it will not be amended. The act indeed says, and I am quoting from section 4:
The Minister of Finance shall, in accordance with the regulations, credit to the account, in each fiscal year,
(a) an amount equal to the contributions paid in that fiscal year . . .
If a member's contributions are automatically doubled then automatically, under the terms of the statute, treasury contributions are doubled. The only body that can ensure that the act will be amended is the government, and I do not yet understand that we have a commitment from the government that this legislation will be amended so the burden will not be automatically doubled as a result of this measure.
